what_its_for: Denosumab is used to treat osteoporosis (weak, brittle bones) in women after menopause and in men at high risk for fractures. It is also used to prevent bone loss caused by certain cancer treatments, and to treat bone problems in people with cancer that has spread to the bones. It works by slowing down the cells that break down bone, helping your bones stay stronger.
how_to_take: Denosumab is given as an injection under the skin (subcutaneous shot) by a doctor, nurse, or other healthcare provider in a clinic or office setting. You will NOT give this injection to yourself at home for Prolia. The shot is usually given in your upper arm, upper thigh, or belly area. Make sure you attend all of your scheduled appointments so you do not miss a dose.
dosing: For Prolia (osteoporosis): The usual dose is 60 mg given as one injection every 6 months. For Xgeva (cancer-related bone conditions): The dose and schedule will be decided by your doctor, but it is often given once a month or every 3 months. Always take calcium and vitamin D supplements as directed by your doctor while on this medication.
missed_dose: If you miss your scheduled injection appointment, contact your doctor or clinic as soon as possible to reschedule. Do not try to skip doses, as stopping denosumab suddenly can increase your risk of spine fractures. After your last dose of Prolia, your doctor may switch you to another bone-strengthening medication to protect you.
storage: Denosumab is stored and handled by your healthcare provider's office or pharmacy. If you are ever given a prefilled syringe to take home, store it in the refrigerator between 36°F and 46°F (2°C to 8°C). Do NOT freeze it. Keep it in the original packaging to protect it from light. If stored at room temperature, use it within 30 days. Do not shake the syringe.
what_to_avoid: Avoid skipping or stopping your injections without talking to your doctor first, as this can lead to serious bone fractures. Try to avoid activities that increase your risk of falls or injuries. Tell your doctor before any dental work or surgery, since denosumab can cause a rare but serious jaw problem called osteonecrosis of the jaw (ONJ). Avoid this medication if you have low calcium levels in your blood — your doctor should check this before starting treatment.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away if you notice: pain, numbness, or tingling in your hands or feet, muscle spasms or cramps, or severe jaw pain or swelling (possible jaw bone problem). Also call if you have: pain or swelling in your thigh, hip, or groin (possible unusual thigh bone fracture), signs of serious infection such as fever, chills, skin redness or swelling, or trouble urinating. Seek emergency care if you have trouble breathing, severe skin rash, or signs of a severe allergic reaction such as swelling of the face, lips, or throat.
when_it_works: Denosumab begins working fairly quickly to slow bone loss, but it may take several months to a year or more before you notice benefits like reduced fracture risk. You may not feel any different, but your doctor will track how well the medication is working through bone density tests (DEXA scans) and blood tests. It is important to keep taking it even if you feel fine.
special_populations: Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Do NOT use denosumab if you are pregnant, as it can harm your unborn baby. Use effective birth control during treatment and for at least 5 months after your last dose. It is not known if denosumab passes into breast milk, so avoid breastfeeding during treatment. Kidney disease: If your kidneys do not work well, you are at higher risk for dangerously low calcium levels. Your doctor will monitor your calcium closely. Children: Denosumab is generally not recommended for children or teenagers, as it can affect bone development. Older adults: Older patients can use denosumab, but fall prevention is especially important to reduce fracture risk.
